## Tours featuring the “Teotihuacan, Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco” excursion

[Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), [Tulpetlac](/mexico/place/tulpetlac/) and [Tlatelolco](/mexico/place/tlatelolco/) are visited on a single excursion day of the [seven-day religious journey through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/). This experience connects the ancient history of Mexico's central highlands with Catholic tradition and concludes with Mass at the Church of St. James.

Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that include this particular [standalone excursion](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-tulpetlac-tlatelolco-pilgrimage/). You are choosing a multi-day itinerary in which the three sites form a carefully planned sequence, rather than just any tour that mentions the pyramids of Teotihuacan.

## Three places, three distinct purposes on the itinerary

Day six begins with a journey to Teotihuacan, an archaeological complex around 60 km northeast of Mexico City. The itinerary includes the Avenue of the Dead, the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, the Citadel and the Temple of Quetzalcoatl. Here visitors encounter a monumental city that flourished long before the Aztec city of Tenochtitlan. The site covers a large area, so comfortable shoes are essential.

The route then continues to [Tulpetlac](/mexico/place/tulpetlac/). The local shrine is associated with the religious tradition of the Virgin of Guadalupe appearing to Juan Bernardino. Unlike the archaeological stop, the significance here lies in the site's place in the history of Catholic devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe.

The final stop is in [Tlatelolco, at the Plaza of the Three Cultures](/mexico/place/tlatelolco/). Archaeological remains of the pre-Hispanic city stand beside the Church of St. James, associated with the later history of colonial Mexico City. The itinerary includes **Holy Mass** in this church. Ending the day here invites reflection on successive historical periods within one city, rather than treating Teotihuacan and Tlatelolco as interchangeable archaeological sites.

| Place | Main focus |
|---|---|
| Teotihuacan | Pre-Hispanic city and pyramids |
| Tulpetlac | Shrine associated with the Guadalupe tradition |
| Tlatelolco | Plaza of the Three Cultures and Mass |

## Where this day fits into the pilgrimage

On the [April 1–7, 2027 itinerary](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), the excursion takes place on **April 6**, day six. Cuernavaca and Taxco are scheduled for the preceding day, while April 7 includes breakfast and an airport transfer. Teotihuacan–Tulpetlac–Tlatelolco is therefore the last major excursion day before departure.

The earlier days cover different places. On April 2, pilgrims visit the Basilica of Guadalupe; on April 3, they explore the historic center of Mexico City, including [Mass at Santo Domingo and a visit to Garibaldi](/mexico/santo-domingo-mexico-city/mexico-city-pilgrimage-garibaldi/). Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla follow, as well as Taxco. The journey includes **five Masses**, private transportation, an English-speaking guide and six nights in Mexico City at the Casa Blanca 4-star hotel or a similar property.

Staying in one city makes luggage logistics easier, but several days involve lengthy excursions from the capital. By the sixth day, participants will have already spent considerable time sightseeing. If you are traveling with older guests or anyone who finds long walks over uneven terrain difficult, discuss the length of the archaeological-site visit and a comfortable pace in advance.

## How this excursion differs from Teotihuacan and Guadalupe

A separate excursion, [“Teotihuacan and the Shrine of Guadalupe”](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/), is included in the [12-day “Viva Mexico” tour](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/). It combines the Basilica of Guadalupe with the ancient city; the longer itinerary continues to Oaxaca and the Yucatán.

The pilgrimage route via **Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco** serves a different purpose. It builds on an earlier visit to the principal Guadalupe shrine, adds another place associated with religious tradition, and ends with Mass. These are not two names for the same excursion. The choice depends on whether you want a single day of cultural sightseeing or a connected pilgrimage through central Mexico.

## What to check before traveling

Teotihuacan is administered by Mexico's INAH. Visiting hours, access to individual structures and any restrictions should be checked before the travel date. Visiting the pyramids as part of the route **does not guarantee that climbing them is permitted**.

Mass in an active church, group transfers and a large archaeological complex all require careful coordination. The [seven-day tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) has specific dates, a set sequence of visits and accompanying services; the standalone excursion has its own description. Before choosing the program, it is worth discussing how long the stops will last and what opportunities there will be to rest during the day.

## Frequently asked questions about the Teotihuacan and Tlatelolco tour

### When does this excursion take place?

On the [April 1–7, 2027 religious journey](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), it is scheduled for **April 6**, day six.

### Where is Mass held?

At the **Church of St. James in Tlatelolco**. This stop follows visits to Teotihuacan and the shrine in Tulpetlac.

### Is this the same as the Teotihuacan and Guadalupe excursion?

No. The [route featuring the Basilica of Guadalupe](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/) is a separate excursion. The pilgrimage day visits Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco, includes Mass and belongs to a different multi-day program.

### Can I visit only the archaeological complex?

For a trip focused on the pyramids, compare [tours of Mexico](/mexico/tour/) and standalone programs around [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/). On this pilgrimage, the archaeological visit is one of three parts of the day.

## Excursions to Teotitlán del Valle: discovering Zapotec weaving

[Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/) in Oaxaca state is known for its family workshops, where wool rugs are woven on wooden looms. Visitors can watch the whole process, from preparing wool and dyeing the yarn to building geometric patterns in the fabric. Seeing the craft firsthand is what makes this excursion different from an ordinary stop at a souvenir market.

We have included Teotitlán in the [“Mitla, Weaving Traditions, Natural Wonders and Mezcal” route](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/). It is a shared **9–10-hour** trip, departing in the morning and visiting several different sites in the Oaxaca Valley with a bilingual guide. The workshop therefore takes up just part of the day, rather than the entire itinerary.

## What happens in a weaving workshop

Teotitlán preserves Zapotec wool-working traditions. An artisan may demonstrate spinning yarn, using natural pigments and setting up patterns on the loom. Red shades are often obtained from cochineal, blue from indigo and yellow from plant dyes. Ask the individual artisan about the significance of a design: not every geometric motif has a single universal meaning.

During the excursion, you will visit a family workshop and see spinning, dyeing and weaving. Buying a rug is entirely your choice and is not listed as an included service.

If textiles are the main reason for your trip, discuss in advance how much time you will have at the workshop. Talking about wool and dyes offers more insight than a quick look at finished rugs. The complexity of handwork becomes especially apparent when you see just how many movements go into a small section of ornament.

## How Teotitlán connects with Mitla and Hierve el Agua

The confirmed itinerary brings together four different stops:

- [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/) — an archaeological complex with geometric stone mosaics;
- [Teotitlán del Valle](/mexico/place/teotitlan-del-valle/) — an introduction to wool textiles and the weavers' craft;
- [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/) — mineral formations resembling frozen waterfalls and views across the valley;
- a visit to a traditional mezcal producer with a tasting.

Each stop speaks to a different interest: history, crafts, nature and gastronomy. Bringing them together in one trip adds variety, although it leaves less time for an in-depth visit to any single site.

Rather than imagining all four stops as one long walk, allow for road transfers around [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) and the conditions of access to natural sites. Check the exact sequence and time spent at each stop against the current itinerary before departure.

## What is included in the Ada Tours excursion

The excursion includes shared transportation, a certified bilingual guide, admission to the specified archaeological sites and Hierve el Agua, and a mezcal tasting. It is conducted in English or Spanish, with departure at approximately **9:00–9:30** and a duration of **9–10 hours**.

Meals, tips and personal expenses are not included. Any wool items you choose to buy are a separate purchase; their cost is not automatically added to the excursion price.

## Which to choose: a craft-focused stop or a full day in the valley

The full route suits first-time visitors to the Oaxaca area who want to see several kinds of attractions. If weaving is your main interest, it is better to discuss a longer visit with an artisan and more time at the family workshop.

Other [culture and history](/interests/culture-and-history/) routes may feature crafts, archaeological sites or city museums. When choosing, look at the actual stops and itinerary rather than relying only on the label “cultural excursion.”

## Frequently asked questions about excursions to Teotitlán

### Can I watch rugs being made?

Yes. The current itinerary includes a visit to a family weaving workshop to see how the textiles are produced.

### How long does the trip take with the other stops?

About 9–10 hours. This is the duration of the full excursion, including Mitla, Teotitlán, Hierve el Agua and a mezcal producer.

### Is buying a rug included?

No. A rug purchase is not among the included services; you may choose and buy items separately if you wish.

### What languages does the guide speak?

English and Spanish are specified for the published excursion.

### Can I spend the entire day at the workshop?

The confirmed itinerary covers several sites. Arranging extra time in Teotitlán requires a separate agreement.

## Excursions to Tlatelolco: Mexico City's history and pilgrimage route

[Tlatelolco and the Plaza of the Three Cultures](/mexico/place/tlatelolco/) bring three periods of Mexican history into one setting: the stone structures of a pre-Hispanic city, the colonial-era Church of Santiago and modern buildings. The stop reveals the passage of centuries without a long journey between separate monuments.

We have included Tlatelolco in the [private “Teotihuacan, Tulpetlac and Tlatelolco” excursion](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-tulpetlac-tlatelolco-pilgrimage/). The day begins at Teotihuacan and continues to the shrine in Tulpetlac; the return to Mexico City includes the Plaza of the Three Cultures and the Church of St. James, where Mass is scheduled.

## Why is it called the Plaza of the Three Cultures?

Ruins of the ancient city survive on the site, with the Church of Santiago nearby and twentieth-century buildings behind it. Together they offer a clear view of pre-Hispanic, colonial and modern Mexico City side by side.

According to Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, Tlatelolco was an important trading center before the Spanish conquest. The archaeological zone contains numerous remains of temples and urban structures. It is especially interesting to compare it with [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), which emerged in a different period and occupied an urban space on an entirely different scale.

The plaza also holds a more recent and painful history: on **October 2, 1968**, members of the student movement were killed there. The site therefore deserves a thoughtful, respectful account not only of its ancient architecture but also of the dramatic events of twentieth-century Mexican history.

## How Tlatelolco fits into the current excursion

At the start of our excursion, you leave Mexico City for the Teotihuacan archaeological complex. The route there covers the Citadel, the Avenue of the Dead, the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, the Temple of Quetzalcoatl and other sites.

The archaeological visit is followed by [Tulpetlac](/mexico/place/tulpetlac/), a pilgrimage stop associated with the tradition of Our Lady of Guadalupe and Juan Bernardino. The route then returns to Mexico City and concludes with Tlatelolco and a visit to the Church of Santiago.

This sequence connects the ancient urban history of the central highlands with religious traditions. Tlatelolco receives a limited portion of the full excursion day; arrange in advance how much time is available to explore individual archaeological remains independently.

## Conditions of the pilgrimage program

This excursion includes **private transportation, an English-speaking guide, admission tickets to the listed attractions and one Holy Mass along the route**. The precise time and place of Mass depend on the church schedule being agreed; the name of the church alone does not establish these arrangements.

Tlatelolco itself also appeals to travelers interested in secular history. This particular excursion, however, is structured as a pilgrimage. If your priority is to spend as much time as possible exploring Mexico City's monuments, compare a different city tour rather than expecting a program that includes Teotihuacan to become an extensive walking tour of the capital.

## Preparing for the visit: clothing, timing and respect for the site

The day combines archaeological sites with an active church. Choose comfortable walking shoes, sun protection and clothing appropriate for a religious setting. Conditions for participating in the service should be agreed with your guide in advance.

The distance to [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) makes the day considerably longer than a standalone visit to the Plaza of the Three Cultures. Consider travel time and the number of stops, not just the list of monuments, when choosing the excursion.

## Frequently asked questions about the excursion to Tlatelolco

### Is Tlatelolco included in the Teotihuacan excursion?

Yes. In the current Ada Tours itinerary, it comes after Teotihuacan and Tulpetlac.

### Can I see three historical periods together?

Yes. Pre-Hispanic ruins, a colonial church and modern buildings stand alongside one another in the plaza.

### Is Mass included?

Yes. One Holy Mass is included in the pilgrimage program. The exact time is agreed separately.

### Is a guide included?

An English-speaking guide is included in this private excursion.

### How much time is set aside specifically for Tlatelolco?

The published description does not specify an exact duration for this stop. It is part of a busy itinerary, rather than a full day devoted to the plaza.

## Excursions to Tlaxcala: monasteries, Ocotlán and Puebla on one route

[Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/) is a historic city in central Mexico, where important attractions are associated with early Franciscan monasteries and local religious traditions. Visitors come for sixteenth-century architecture, peaceful city squares and shrines in and around the city.

We offer the [private “Shrines of Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla” route](/mexico/tlaxcala/tlaxcala-ocotlan-puebla-pilgrimage/). It goes beyond a city tour: it begins at [San Miguel del Milagro](/mexico/place/san-miguel-del-milagro/), continues to a monastery and basilica in the Tlaxcala area, and concludes its cultural program in Puebla.

## Tlaxcala's Franciscan complex and UNESCO heritage

One of the principal stops is the [San Francisco monastery](/mexico/place/san-francisco-tlaxcala/) and the Cathedral of the Assumption. The complex dates to the early decades of the colonial era, when Franciscans established religious centers across central Mexico.

In **2021**, UNESCO added Tlaxcala's Franciscan monastery and cathedral ensemble to the expanded World Heritage property “Earliest 16th-Century Monasteries on the Slopes of Popocatepetl.” This designation applies to the historic ensemble itself, not to the entire excursion or every building in the city.

The early monastery's architecture, courtyard, stone walls and history as an important religious center are all worth exploring. This visit offers a contrast to the elaborate Baroque architecture of later centuries.

## Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán: a different architectural language

Another major site is the [Basilica of Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/), an outstanding example of local Baroque architecture. Its richly decorated façades and interiors stand in sharp contrast to the more restrained early monastic complex.

Inside are the main altar, the venerated image of Our Lady and the Camerín, associated with dressing the statue for religious ceremonies. Accounts of the image's miraculous origins belong to church tradition rather than established historical fact.

On a pilgrimage, it is important to leave time not only for photographs but also for a quiet visit inside the church. Access arrangements may differ during services, ceremonies or preparations within the building.

## Why the route begins at San Miguel del Milagro

The first stop on our route is the [Shrine of San Miguel del Milagro](/mexico/place/san-miguel-del-milagro/). It is associated with the tradition that the Archangel Michael appeared to Diego Lázaro here in 1631. Holy Mass is scheduled at this site.

The route then continues to Tlaxcala, including the San Francisco monastery and Ocotlán. Its sequence is guided primarily by the purpose of the pilgrimage: several shrines form a connected journey, rather than a random collection of architectural landmarks.

## Puebla: continuing beyond Tlaxcala

After Ocotlán, you travel to [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/). The itinerary includes the [cathedral](/mexico/place/puebla-cathedral/) and the [Church of Santo Domingo with the Chapel of the Rosary](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/). These are landmarks of a substantial colonial city in their own right, so a trip that includes them cannot be described simply as a tour of Tlaxcala.

When selecting this itinerary, consider the distances between towns, the time needed at each church and the return journey to Mexico City. An exact duration is not specified in advance; it needs to be coordinated with your travel date and the schedule of services.

## What is included and who the route suits

Our excursion includes **private transportation, an English-speaking guide, admission tickets to the listed sites and one Holy Mass**. This list does not imply that meals or fixed times for all religious services are included.

The route is particularly suited to travelers interested in Mexico's Catholic heritage. Architecture enthusiasts will also appreciate comparing Tlaxcala's early monastic complex, the Baroque Basilica of Ocotlán and Puebla's city churches in one day. If you want to focus on a single site, discussing a shorter, dedicated trip makes more sense than trying to examine every shrine in depth in one visit.

## Frequently asked questions about excursions to Tlaxcala

### Which shrines are included in the confirmed route?

San Miguel del Milagro, the San Francisco monastery, the Basilica of Ocotlán, Puebla Cathedral and the Church of Santo Domingo with the Chapel of the Rosary.

### Is Tlaxcala's monastery really on the UNESCO list?

Yes. The Franciscan ensemble was added to the expanded World Heritage property in 2021.

### Is Mass included?

Yes. One Holy Mass is included along the route, associated with the visit to San Miguel del Milagro.

### What transportation is provided?

The current program specifies private transportation and an English-speaking guide.

### Are lunch and personal expenses included?

They are not listed among the included services in the published information. The arrangements are agreed separately before the trip.

## Shrines of Tlaxcala, Ocotlán and Puebla: a tour of Mexico's churches

Our pilgrimage route connects [Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/tlaxcala/), the shrine of San Miguel del Milagro, the [Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/) and the historic churches of [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/). Travelers depart from Mexico City in the morning and return to the capital after visiting the shrines.

The itinerary is designed to explore the Catholic history of central Mexico. It operates **as a private excursion with an English-speaking guide and transportation**, including admission to the listed attractions and **one Holy Mass**.

## Shrine of San Miguel del Milagro

The first stop is [San Miguel del Milagro](/mexico/place/san-miguel-del-milagro/). According to church tradition, the Archangel Michael appeared here to Diego Lázaro in 1631. This event is the basis for local devotion to the shrine.

**Holy Mass** is held here during the excursion. Participants should prepare in advance for a visit to an active place of worship by following the instructions of church staff, dressing appropriately and observing photography rules during the service.

## San Francisco monastery and the Basilica of Ocotlán

After the shrine, the route continues to the [San Francisco monastery in Tlaxcala](/mexico/place/san-francisco-tlaxcala/). Its history is linked to the early colonial period and the spread of Catholicism in the region.

The next stop is the [Basilica of Our Lady of Ocotlán](/mexico/place/ocotlan-basilica/), known for its expressive Baroque architecture. Another feature of the complex is the **Camerín**, the room where the revered image of the Virgin Mary is dressed for religious ceremonies. According to local tradition, the image of Our Lady was miraculously discovered in a tree.

The history of the shrine is presented as religious tradition, while its Baroque architecture and physical layout are historical and cultural features that visitors can observe. Making this distinction allows us to speak respectfully about faith while keeping the account accurate.

## Puebla: the cathedral and the Chapel of the Rosary

The second part of the day takes you to [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/), whose historic center is renowned for colonial architecture. Here you visit the [Cathedral](/mexico/place/puebla-cathedral/) and the [Church of Santo Domingo with the Chapel of the Rosary](/mexico/place/puebla-santo-domingo-rosary-chapel/).

The Chapel of the Rosary is famous for its elaborate decorative interior. Together with the cathedral and the churches of Tlaxcala, it shows how religious art and Baroque traditions developed in different cities of central Mexico.

After Puebla, the group returns to Mexico City. This is **a route through several towns and cities**, so the exact transfer schedule, stops and total length of the day need to be agreed in advance.

## Included services and practical recommendations

The excursion includes **private transportation, an English-speaking guide, admission tickets to the listed sites and one Mass**. Meals, the price and the return time are not specified separately in the excursion conditions.

Comfortable shoes, water and sun protection will be useful on this long day; modest clothing is appropriate for the churches. Given the number of shrines, it is more rewarding to spend meaningful time at the listed sites than to add extra stops along the way.

## Frequently asked questions about the pilgrimage to Tlaxcala and Puebla

### Where is Holy Mass scheduled?

At the **Shrine of San Miguel del Milagro**, the route's first major stop.

### Which churches are included?

The San Francisco monastery, the Basilica of Ocotlán, Puebla Cathedral and Santo Domingo with the Chapel of the Rosary; San Miguel del Milagro is another separate stop.

### Where does the excursion end?

After visiting Puebla, the itinerary includes **a return to Mexico City**.

### What language does the guide speak?

An **English-speaking guide** is confirmed for this private excursion.

### Is this a short walk through one city?

No. The route connects **several settlements and church complexes**, so travel and worship require adequate time.
